I’ve felt low for a little over three years now. It’s like a gray film over everything. I cry at the smallest things—someone returning a late book, a sad line in a novel—and sometimes I have to duck into the staff restroom because I can’t stop the tears. 

My job is usually about focus, but lately I’ll read the same paragraph over and over and it just won’t stick. I lose my place shelving, drift off in the middle of helping patrons, and then I beat myself up for it. I replay tiny mistakes—misplacing a book, snapping at a coworker—and tell myself I’m incompetent, that this is why I’m still alone at 49.

It’s not always like this, though. A few times over these years I’ve had these stretches—about four or five days at a time—where I feel unusually “switched on.” I sleep maybe three hours and still wake up buzzing with ideas: reorganizing entire sections of the library, starting big projects at home. I talk much faster, my thoughts race, and coworkers say I seem “wired.” I don’t do anything outrageous, but I’m noticeably different, and then I crash back into that long, dragging low mood again.
D014-D009_h023.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D014-D009_h024.question:
I’ve pretty much felt low for the last three years, like this gray mood I can’t shake. I get teary over small stuff, like if a customer snaps at me or I make a tiny mistake with the register, I’ll have to step into the back because I feel like I’m about to cry. It’s embarrassing.  

My head feels foggy a lot of the time. At the station, I’ll stare at the pump screen and have to reread the numbers, or I’ll forget what a customer just asked for. It’s like I’m moving through mud, mentally. I keep replaying dumb things I’ve done—like being late once or messing up change—and I tear into myself over it for days, calling myself useless, a screwup.  

But then, every so often, I’ll have these times—like last spring for about four or five days—where I barely sleep, maybe two hours a night, and I’m still wired. I talk a mile a minute, feel amazing, start planning big things like quitting my job, starting a business, texting everyone nonstop. My manager even told me I was “acting jacked up or on something.” Then it crashes back into that long, low, cloudy feeling.
D014-D009_h024.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D014-D009_h025.question:
I guess the low stuff has been going on a little over three years now, since about a year after my wife passed. I’m on the verge of tears most days, sometimes for no obvious reason. I’ll be at my desk trying to read through COBOL from the ’80s and suddenly I’m choking up. I feel like I second‑guess every choice I make—at work, with money, even what to eat. I keep asking my younger colleagues to double‑check my changes because I don’t trust my own judgment anymore.

My memory feels worse, too. I’ll put a spec sheet down and five minutes later I’m wandering around the office looking for it, or I forget why I walked into a room. I don’t think it’s dementia or anything; it’s more like my brain is foggy. It’s made me slower and I’ve missed a couple of production issues I would’ve caught before.

But then there are these spells—every so often, for a few days, I feel “switched on.” I sleep maybe three, four hours and don’t feel tired. I talk fast, take on extra projects, refactor code overnight, spend a bunch of money on new hardware I don’t really need. It feels great in the moment, almost too good, and each time it gets me into trouble at work or financially. These episodes have happened several times over the years, not just once, and they’re very different from my usual low, dragged‑out state.
D014-D009_h025.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
